claims.text: Atomic size mismatch in multi-component concentrated alloys produces local lattice distortion.
The magnitude of local lattice distortion governs the strength and deformation behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by local lattice distortion increases yield strength.
Local lattice distortion alters strain-hardening behavior.
Excessive atomic size mismatch can create localized stress concentrations.
Localized stress concentrations caused by excessive mismatch can reduce ductility and cause early or brittle failure.
Increased atomic size differences impede both dislocation nucleation and dislocation glide through enhanced local lattice distortion.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can quantify the relevant local lattice distortions.
Transmission electron microscopy can directly image the relevant local strain fields.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have greater local lattice distortion than lower-mismatch baseline alloys.
Alloys with greater quantified local lattice distortion will exhibit higher yield strength than same-structure, lower-mismatch baseline alloys.
Alloys with greater quantified local lattice distortion will exhibit altered strain-hardening profiles relative to the baseline.
At sufficiently high lattice distortion, increased strength will be accompanied by reduced ductility or earlier failure.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold at room temperature and moderate strain rates in single-phase solid-solution alloys.
The proposed relationship may not govern deformation when secondary phases or high-temperature creep mechanisms dominate.
Chemical short-range order and stacking-fault-energy variations can also influence mechanical behavior.
